Elastic Properties and Deformation Mechanisms in the van der Waals Single Crystalline Indium Selenide Qi Zheng1,2, Chengyao Liang1, Jinyang Jiang2, Shaofan Li 1*

1 Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, University of California Berkeley, Berkeley, California 94720, United States 2 School of Materials Science and Engineering, Southeast University, Nanjing 211189, P.R. China Abstract The bulk van der Waals (vdW) single crystalline indium selenide (β-InSe) displays exceptional plasticity in a layered crystalline form at both micro and macroscale. However, the atomic origin of deformation mechanism and plasticity remains unclear. Here, we report an atomic-level study on the deformation mechanisms of InSe by using first-principles calculations. Remarkable anisotropic elasticity is observed in the van der Waals InSe layered crystals, and the stiffness is dramatically softened because of the vdW gap in the layered structure. The density functional theory (DFT) simulations capture the distinct fracture modes in the uniaxial tensile deformation, depending on the loading directions-- brittle fracture in the [100] and [110] directions and ductile failure in the [001] direction. The InSe layered crystal structure exhibits superplastic deformability under uniaxial compression. Different transition pathways, including interlayer tangling, amorphization, and crosslinking, are tracked along respective deformation directions. The unprecedented plasticity of InSe layered crystals can be attributed to the phase transition coupled with interlayer gliding and cross-layer dislocation slipping. This study deepens our understanding of the deformation mechanisms of layered materials at the atomistic level, and it provides insights on tailoring material properties for low-dimensional material design based on its deformation mechanism. Keywords: Indium (II) selenide (InSe); 2D materials; First-principles calculations; Elastic moduli; Deformation mechanism; Plasticity, van der Waals material. 1. These vdW materials offer unprecedented properties and unique functionalities; for example, many fascinating electrical, optical, and magnetic properties have recently been reported in different layered van der Waals crystal structures.[4–7] Most vdW materials are intrinsically brittle at room temperature, limiting their applications, such as being used in flexible electronics.[8,9] The vdW material may also exhibit plasticity behaviors.[10] For example, inorganic α- Ag2S exhibits exceptional metal-like ductility at room temperature.[11] A flexible thermoelectric power generation module has been designed by exploiting the novel mechanical properties.[12] More recently, superplastic deformability in the singlecrystalline indium selenide (InSe) has been reported.[13] The discovery of intrinsic plasticity in Ag2S and InSe has opened new avenues for fundamental scientific studies and applied device designs. However, the underlying mechanisms remain mysterious, especially at the atomic level, which hinders the search and design for ductile vdW materials. In this work, we investigated the mechanical properties of the van der Waals InSe single crystal using first-principles calculations at the atomic scale. The bonding and elastic properties of InSe were modeled and studied based on the optimized atomic structure, further validated by the experimental results. The average elastic moduli were estimated using the micromechanics homogenization method, the Voigt-Reuss- Hill approximation scheme particularly. Moreover, we reported the ideal compressive and tensile strength by applying uniaxial deformation along different directions. Distinct failure modes were captured, and they can be explained by the interlayer gliding and dislocation slipping. We examined the deformation mechanisms and discovered new pathways induced by phase transitions. The results of this work revealed the unique mechanical properties of layered InSe single crystal, and it offers atomistic scale insights into the mechanical behaviors of low-dimensional materials. 2. Methods We performed first-principles calculations using the Vienna Ab Initio Simulation Package (VASP)[14,15] with the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) comprising van der Waals corrections (DFT-D3 method in this work).[16,17] The projector augmented wave (PAW) method[18,19] combined with the Perdew-Burke- Ernzerhof exchange[20] was used throughout the calculation. The plane-wave basis energy cutoff was set at 500 eV for high precision, and the related criteria were set 10-5 eV for total energy change and 10-3 eV/Å for the force on each atom. The Gamma grids in the Brillouin zone of the primitive cells were set as 12×12×3 for the k-point sampling. The elastic constants, Cij, were calculated based on the stress-strain relation method. Some elastic moduli were derived from the Voigt-Reuss-Hill approximation scheme. The sample thickness was considered as 50 nm throughout the diffraction simulation. 3. Results and Discussions Here, β phase InSe single crystal was studied, which adopts a space group of P63/mmc. In Figure 1A, the van der Waals InSe bulk crystal features a layered structure, and each layer takes the In-Se honeycomb lattice in the ab plane. Meanwhile, there exists a vdW gap between the adjacent layers in the c direction. These layers are stacked along the c axis at 8.38 Å (c/2, where c is the optimized lattice constant along the c axis), separated by the Se and Se atoms. Different layerstacking modes can lead to various InSe polytypes,[24–26] including β-InSe,[27] and γ- InSe.[28]

We think it is best to characterize this ductile deformation mechanism as the cohesive deformation mechanism because the vdW gap behaves like a cohesive spring that facilitates interlayer separation, which may be the primary mechanism for such ductile failure, as shown in Figure 3D. Moreover, we employed uniaxial compression on InSe single crystalline layer structures. In Figure 4A, serrations in the stress-strain curves can be found in simulations and experimental results, indicating the dislocation nucleation, crosslink, and break-off. Large plastic deformability is also confirmed in the uniaxial compression simulations along different directions. We observed that the average bond length of In-Se increased from 2.65 Å to ~2.8 Å throughout the deformation (Figure 4B). The In-Se bond stretched by ~15%, reflecting its magnificent flexibility, which can be attributed to the huge plasticity of the InSe single crystal. Meanwhile, a huge discrepancy of In-Se bond length at a bigger deviation value represented by the shadow can be noticed at the late deformation, supporting the local heterogeneity would induce phase transformation or amorphization.[44] Many specifics, a remarkable compressive strength up to 50 GPa is noted along the [100] direction. We found that the compression along different directions can be categorized into several stages by tracking the corresponding structural configurations in the deformation pathways.[45] For example, the hexagonal InSe lattice distorts into a semi-rhombic structure by transferring the loading along the In-Se skeleton, resulting in the first peak along the [100] compression direction. Moreover, the second peak can be assigned to the formation of complicated superlattices owing to interlayer glide and dislocation. Finally, the InSe crystal deforms into a triclinic lattice induced by the cross-layer slipping (Figure 4E). We also observed the structural phase transition under compressive deformations. In Figure 4F, crystalline InSe undergoes amorphization under compression. Consequently, the amorphous InSe manifests an extensive plastic deformation range with a longer elongation before failure. It is recognized that the mechanical properties can be distinct amorphous states such as glassy metal,[46] high-entropy-alloy,[47] and amorphous silica.[48] Figure 4C displays the simulated XRD pattern of the InSe single crystal. The intense peak at 21.2o is the [004] reflection, which is significant in the β-InSe crystal.[49] Here, we measured the intensity evolution of the [004] facet throughout the [110] deformation in Figure 4D. Note that the amorphization process occurs rapidly once the crystal reaches its critical disorder state[50] --at 0.22 compression strain in our case. Interestingly, layered InSe can be transformed into the crosslinked bulk crystal at extreme compression conditions. In particular, fresh In-Se, In-In bonds are established between the interlayers (Figure 4G) that can be the main load-bearing component to maintain the structural integrity. These formed bonds can predominately reinforce the InSe structure by introducing dislocations upon the loading,[51,52] and thus, it enhances the fracture toughness. Generally, the InSe single layers are stretched to turn flat at the compression stress of 4.5 GPa at the initial period. Afterward, the vdW gap between the layers is continuously narrowed and finally gets attached when In-Se, In-In bonds are generated in the inter-spacing. This finding provides opportunities to manipulate 2D materials into bulk crosslinked materials with desirable properties through mechanical compression. We postulate that the interlayer gliding and dislocation slip throughout the structural phase transition and dictate the exceptional plasticity of layered InSe single crystal. 4. Conclusions In this work, we investigated the properties of β phase InSe single crystal layer structure by using first-principles calculations. The atomic structure, elastic moduli, and deformation mechanisms were examined, which have deepened our understanding of van der Waals layered materials under mechanical loading. Some conclusions can be reached as follows: (1) The van der Waals single crystalline InSe exhibits remarkable anisotropic elasticity owing to its layered features. The c crystallographic direction has a softer stiffness at 35.4 GPa, because of the vdW gap between the interlayers. The calculated average elastic moduli are K= 25.1, G= 11.8, and E= 30.6 GPa, where K, G, and E are the isotropic bulk, shear, and Young’s moduli, accordingly. (2) Distinct fracture modes are observed in the tensile deformation. The single crystalline InSe layer structure possesses brittle failure mode in the [100] and [110] directions, whereas cohesive ductile failure mode is observed in the [001] direction, which can be attributed to the In-Se bond network in the ab plane, and the long-range vdW forces resided in the interlayer, respectively. (3) The van der Waals single crystal InSe displays superb plasticity under uniaxial compression. The exceptional plasticity of layered InSe single crystal may be enabled by the structure phase transition coupled with interlayer gliding and cross-layer dislocation slipping throughout the entire loading cycle. This work offers an atomic understanding of the deformation mechanisms of the layered InSe crystal.
